text: Isolation cuts off a host's network access while leaving it running — that part's a solved technical problem, covered already in the EDR lesson. What's much harder is deciding when to actually pull that trigger on a system where isolation itself causes damage, because stopping the attacker and taking the business offline can turn out to be the exact same action.

Isolating a workstation almost never matters to the business. Isolating the one production database every order on the website writes to is a very different call — security may stop the attacker cold and take the entire business offline in the same moment. That's why isolation decisions on critical systems require business judgment, not just technical confidence.

A real decision weighs several things at once: how confident the team is this is an active, spreading compromise; how much worse it gets if nothing happens right now; what the outage itself costs in revenue, safety, or regulatory exposure for every minute it's down; and whether a narrower compensating control — blocking one port, disabling one account — could reduce the risk without the full cost of isolation.

Because a wrong call cuts both ways — too slow and the attacker keeps moving, too fast and the business eats an unnecessary outage — most real IR plans route high-impact isolation decisions through a named authority: an IR commander, a CISO, or the business owner. The analyst's job is presenting the technical facts fast enough for that person to decide, not unilaterally pulling the plug on a revenue-critical system.

Take the identical technical finding — ransomware precursor activity — showing up at a hospital's patient-records server at 2 a.m. and at a retailer's point-of-sale system during its biggest sale. The hospital authorizes isolation immediately; patient safety outweighs almost any other cost. The retailer asks for a few minutes to confirm a lower-cost option first. Same finding, genuinely different business realities. Next up: containing a compromised account versus a compromised host.
